Modular Arithmetic Tables

DivisibilityNumber TheoryAlgebra
Game: Look at the table of an operation where numbers wrap around, like the hours on a clock. See what patterns hide in it.
How to play: Choose +, ×, − or ÷ and slide the modulus. Press a number in the table to light up all the same numbers. Division works only when the modulus is a prime number.
Operation
Look for the math

Two numbers are congruent modulo N when they leave the same remainder on division by N. Doing arithmetic with only the N remainders works for adding, subtracting and multiplying. The tables show what it is like. Every statement here was checked by the test for every modulus from 2 to 30.

Addition and subtraction

Each row of an addition table is the one above it with every entry moved one place round, a circular rotation. If N is odd, the main diagonal (a + a = 2a) holds every remainder once; if N is even, it holds only half of them, each twice. In a subtraction table with an odd number of rows the second diagonal is a rearrangement of the first row.

Multiplication, and why primes are special

The tables leave out 0. When N is prime, every row and every column is a rearrangement of the first, so a product never repeats within a row: you can always undo a multiplication, which means division works. Press a number: it appears exactly once in each row and each column, a solution of the rook problem (N rooks that cannot capture one another). The 1 is in both corners of the main diagonal and nowhere else, and 6 ÷ 5 = 4 mod 7 because 4 × 5 = 20 = 6 mod 7. Both diagonals of a multiplication table read the same in both directions, and for a prime modulus the main diagonal holds half the remainders (the squares), each twice.

When N is not prime

Then rows have zeros and repeats. Mod 10, 5 × 1, 5 × 3, 5 × 5, 5 × 7 and 5 × 9 are all 5, so "5 ÷ 5" has no single answer, and 5 × 2, 5 × 4, 5 × 6 and 5 × 8 are all 0, which never happens with ordinary numbers. A row is a rearrangement of the first row exactly when its number has no common factor with N (the test confirmed this in both directions for every N, so the page's remark that "the reverse is wrong" does not hold for these tables).

Compare N = 7 and N = 8 with ×. Which table has a row that is a rearrangement of the first? How many of them are there for N = 8?
